dhpak2.7:1.1: The Pāli calls this Maghavatthu, the story of Magha; the earlier English title named Mahāli's questions. The romanized heading Mahālipañhavatthu and editorial headings ‘Story of the Present,’ ‘Story of the Past,’ ‘A Path to Heaven,’ ‘A King’s Apology,’ ‘A Pinnacle for Posterity,’ ‘Reborn as Sakka,’ ‘The Realm of the Thirty-Three,’ ‘Sakka’s Former Wives,’ and ‘The Fruit of Heedlessness’ were removed because they have no separate local Pāli counterparts.
dhpak2.7:3.1: licchavī does not itself call Mahāli a prince; the English description was corrected.
dhpak2.7:4.2: māṇavo means youth. The repeated English description of Magha as a ‘prince’ changed the Pāli meaning.
dhpak2.7:4.3: The redundant second ‘in a previous state of existence’ in the explanation of Purindada was removed.
dhpak2.7:4.11: The divine wife is Sujā in the Pāli, not Sujātā.
dhpak2.7:5.8: The English vow ‘Should anger spring up within me, may I quickly suppress it’ follows SN 11.13:13.9 (khippameva naṃ paṭivineyyanti). The local VRI quotation khippameva na paṭivineyya appears to contain a textual error that reverses the vow; the Pāli JSON preserves the VRI reading.
dhpak2.7:7.1: The Teacher's connective statement about explaining the dangers of heedlessness and benefits of heedfulness is Pāli-only under this key.
dhpak2.7:8.1: Magha is a youth (māṇava), not a prince.
dhpak2.7:9.4: Magha supplied water in hot weather as well as fire in cold weather (gimhakāle udakaṃ).
dhpak2.7:9.5: Magha's thought that a pleasant place is dear to everyone (ramaṇīyaṃ ṭhānaṃ nāma sabbesaṃ piyaṃ) was restored.
dhpak2.7:11.1: kudālādihatthā means they carried spades and other tools; it does not specifically name axes.
dhpak2.7:13.4: Magha tells the thirty-three to direct loving-kindness toward themselves (attani ca) as well as the king, headman, and elephant.
dhpak2.7:19.6: issarānaṃ identifies the powerful, not specifically kings, as users of one section of the hall.
dhpak2.7:21.1: koviḷārarukkha is the koviḷāra tree, not an ebony tree.
dhpak2.7:28.1: asurā vasanti says Asuras dwelt in Tāvatiṃsa; the English had placed both devas and Asuras there at that point.
dhpak2.7:28.2: The Asuras prepared celestial drink; the English had added ‘for them.’
dhpak2.7:28.4: Sakka asks why he should share his kingdom with the Asuras (imehi), not with ‘these Devaputtas.’
dhpak2.7:28.7: The Asura palace arose at the foot of Sineru (asuravimānaṃ nāma nibbatti); the earlier English wrongly put it ‘in the palace.’
dhpak2.7:29.10: The central banner, three hundred leagues high (majjhe ṭhito dhajo tiyojanasatubbedho), had been missing from the English account.
dhpak2.7:30.1: The koviḷāra tree's resulting coral tree measures three hundred leagues around (tiyojanasataparimaṇḍalo), not one hundred.
dhpak2.7:30.3: The Paṇḍukambala stone throne was misnamed ‘Yellowstone’; its color is compared with the jayasumana flower.
dhpak2.7:30.4: upaḍḍhakāyo pavisati says half of Sakka's body sinks into the throne, not half the throne's mass into the ground.
dhpak2.7:30.8: tigāvutaaḍḍhayojanappamāṇe means two or three quarters of a league around, not a range from half to three quarters.
dhpak2.7:31.10: attano kumbhe ratanapallaṅke nisīdiṃsu says the thirty-three gods sat on jeweled couches in their respective vessels; the English had omitted this and repeated that Erāvaṇa made the vessels.
dhpak2.7:32.3: māsassa aṭṭha divase says the Sudhammā hall hosts a Dhamma hearing on eight days of the month, not only on the eighth day.
dhpak2.7:32.7: uppannapubbanimitte means the gods had the prior signs of impending death; mohayamānā says the grove charms them, rather than their simply walking about rejoicing.
dhpak2.7:33.1: The earlier English explicitly called the other women Sakka's wives; the Pāli says they were reborn near him (mameva santike nibbattā). The heading ‘Sakka’s Former Wives’ was removed.
dhpak2.7:34.4: mameva santike nibbattā says the other women were reborn near Sakka; the English explicitly called them his wives.
dhpak2.7:38.4: mama santike nibbattissasi is Sakka's promise that Sujā would be reborn near him; the English explicitly called her one of his wives at this point.
dhpak2.7:39.2: The Pāli attributes Sujā's rebirth as a potter's daughter to her precepts but does not say it was ‘solely’ because of them.
dhpak2.7:40.2: The market visitors brought pulses and the like (muggamāsādīni), not coins.
dhpak2.7:40.5: The visitors ask whether the precepts are black or blue (kāḷaṃ ... nīlādivaṇaṃ), not brown.
dhpak2.7:41.3: avijahitapañcasīlā means Sujā had not abandoned the five precepts; the Pāli does not call her a maiden.
dhpak2.7:45.1: Mātali identifies the crying birds as Garuḍa fledglings (garuḷapotakā).
dhpak2.7:47.6: ārakkhaṃ adāsi says Sakka provided protection to each group, beginning with the Nāgas; the English had posted a guard to defend only the Nāgas.
dhpak2.7:49.1: The repeated Pāli transcription of verse 30 was removed because it has no separate local Pāli counterpart; the English verse translation remains.
dhpak2.7:50.1: The full Pāli explanation of verse 30 has no English translation and remains Pāli-only under this paragraph.
dhpak2.7:52.1: The Pāli closing title Maghavatthu sattamaṃ is Pāli-only and has no English key.
